content.intro: This lesson covers Table Design and Data Integrity as part of Excel Tables and Structured References. It follows the attached Excel curriculum, with an emphasis on small examples and verification.
content.why_it_matters: Table Design and Data Integrity supports repeatable analysis by organizing, cleaning, summarizing, or relating data. Preserve the raw source and reconcile a summary back to its input records.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Table Design and Data Integrity focuses on the following parts of the supplied syllabus: Consistent column names; Avoiding merged headers; Managing blank rows and duplicate records; Designing append-friendly datasets. Keep the underlying source data visible and make each assumption explicit.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus coverage
items: Managing blank rows and duplicate records

content_blocks.code: Input rows → validate types/keys → sort or filter a copy → reconcile row counts and totals
content_blocks.expected_output: Shows a repeatable data-management sequence that keeps the original data available for comparison.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Preserve a raw-data copy, confirm selected columns and sort order, and verify that record counts and unique identifiers still match expectations.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Work in a duplicate workbook or a scratch sheet. Restore the input range and formula/code to the original state, clear filters or selections, then rerun the same test cases. Record expected and actual behavior rather than assuming a successful result.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with a small, known dataset for table design and data integrity. Apply the example above, compute or inspect at least one result independently, then deliberately try a blank, duplicate, boundary, or not-found case where relevant.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small worksheet or workbook section that demonstrates table design and data integrity. Use clear headers, label units and assumptions, and capture expected versus actual output for a normal case and an edge case. Where the concept requires a specialized Excel feature, first verify that feature is available in your Excel edition.

content.task: Build or inspect an Excel example that demonstrates table design and data integrity; use the example to verify one normal and one edge case, and write down any version or tool dependency. For a complete curriculum practice scenario, also complete “Inventory Management Sheet” using the synthetic dataset `assets/data/practical-11-inventory-management-sheet.csv`; see the linked additional exercise file.
task_acceptance_criteria: The worksheet/workflow uses a clear, labeled source range and explicit assumptions.
The learner records an expected output and independently compares it with the actual result.
At least one relevant edge case is checked; data and formula errors are not silently concealed.
The workbook is saved as a copy and compatibility/security/accessibility notes are followed where relevant.
hints: Reduce the problem to a small range with known values before scaling it up.
Inspect cell values and formulas, not only displayed formatting; verify data types, references and range boundaries.
Compare expected versus actual results and check the Microsoft documentation for version-specific functions or tools.
content.expected_output: Shows a repeatable data-management sequence that keeps the original data available for comparison.
common_mistakes: Assuming the displayed format is the same as the stored value or data type.
Using an incorrect range boundary, a mismatched lookup key, or an unverified assumption.
Trusting a result without comparing it with a known calculation or checking a failure/edge case.
summary: Table Design and Data Integrity supports the workflow in Excel Tables and Structured References.
Use a small example, make assumptions visible, and verify the result against the source.
Check target-version availability and keep a clean copy before making high-impact changes.
